In summary, our research is concerned with
the way in which the Australian Public Service (APS) is structured to deal with policy issues, the way in which it is organized, and the way in which policy decisions are taken and implemented.
how public servants make decisions, how they make sense of what they are doing and the implications for policy outcomes.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
decision-making in the public service is not as it should be.
the APS is not a rational decision-making body.

(a) decision making in the Australian public service is rational in the sense that it is guided by a set of principles which can be described in a logical and consistent manner; (b) decision making in Australian public service is also rational in the sense of being based on the best information available at the time; and (c) decision making in this service is also rational, in the sense that the process is open to scrutiny and challenge, both within and outside the service.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the APS has been successful at managing its internal processes but less successful at managing the external environment.
the APS is a rational, but not always rational, actor.
we have developed a model of the decision-making process that can be applied to a range of policy areas and that we can identify the key actors in that process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
decision-making within the Australian Public service is not a simple matter of following the right procedure or of applying the right technique.
the Australian Public Service needs to be more open to different ways of thinking about policy problems and more willing to experiment with different approaches to decision-making.
the Australian Public Service is more than a set of procedures.
